definition.text: Turning waste or unwanted products into new materials or products seen as having greater quality or value, such as artistic or environmental value.

facts.text: It is a subset of recycling that adds value, unlike downcycling, which turns waste into lower-quality products.
Before the Industrial Revolution, upcycling to repair goods was common; mass production and a linear model of throwing things away reduced it.
The terms upcycling and downcycling first appeared in print in a 1994 SalvoNEWS article.
It is a circular economy strategy that cuts resource use by raising product value and extending product lifespans through repair and repurposing.
In poorer countries it reflects a lack of access to new goods; in rich countries, more concern for the environment.

definition.text: Recovering rare metals from a society's stockpile of discarded electronic waste, its 'urban mine', by mechanical and chemical treatment.

facts.text: A 2010 Japanese government study estimated 6,800 tonnes of gold could be recovered from used electronics in Japan.
Its main aim is recovering materials, whereas landfill mining aims to fix problems at the disposal site.
In developing countries e-waste is often recycled informally, even inside homes, without proper equipment.
Shifting from primary production to urban mining needs detailed accounts of materials in use and in obsolete stocks.

definition.text: Giving economic value to waste or residues by reusing or recycling them into useful materials.

facts.text: It usually means using the residue of one industrial process as raw material or energy for another.
Industrial wastes suit it best because they are more consistent and predictable than household waste.
Interest grew with tighter regulation of residues and the spread of sustainable development and circular economy ideas in the 1990s and 2000s.
Mine tailings, red mud from alumina production, and even spent nuclear fuel can be valorised.

definition.text: Turning food waste into food or feed products, or extracting food or feed ingredients from it.

facts.text: Landfilled food waste releases methane and other harmful compounds.
Food wastes can yield biofertilisers, bioplastics, biofuels, chemicals and nutraceuticals, and can be converted into insect protein.
About 30% of the food livestock eat comes from food waste or crops grown and processed in the supply chain.
